etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French passage, from passer (“to pass”).

definitions.definition: A paragraph or section of text or music with particular meaning.
Part of a path or journey.
An incident or episode.

quote.citation: 1961, United States. Congress. House. Committee on Foreign Affairs, Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961: Hearings:
quote.text: But there are those who do not feel that the sordid passages of life should be kept off the stage. It is a matter of opinion.

definitions.definition: The official approval of a bill or act by a parliament. [from 17th c.]
The advance of time.

quote.citation: 2011, Roy F. Baumeister, John Tierney, Willpower, →ISBN, page 209:
quote.text: The passage of decades has not erased the value of parental monitoring.

definitions.definition: (art) The use of tight brushwork to link objects in separate spatial plains. Commonly seen in Cubist works.
A passageway or corridor.
(nautical) A strait or other narrow waterway.
(caving) An underground cavity, formed by water or falling rocks, which is much longer than it is wide.
(euphemistic) The vagina.

quote.citation: 1986, Bertrice Small, A Love for All Time‎[1], New American Library, →ISBN, page 463:
quote.text: With a look of triumph that he was unable to keep from his dark eyes he slid into her passage with one smooth thrust,  […]

quote.citation: 1987, Usha Sarup, Expert Lovemaking, Jaico Publishing House, →ISBN, page 53:
quote.text: This way, the tip of your penis will travel up and down her passage.

quote.citation: 2009, Cat Lindler, Kiss of a Traitor, Medallion Press, →ISBN, page 249:
quote.text: At the same moment, Aidan plunged two fingers deep into her passage and broke through her fragile barrier.

definitions.definition: The act of passing; movement across or through.

quote.text: He claimed that he felt the passage of the knife through the ilio-cæcal valve, from the very considerable pain which it caused.

quote.citation: 1954 February, “Notes and News: Deviation  at Bramwith”, in Railway Magazine, page 137:
quote.text: When the scheme is completed, the 99-year-old swing bridge over the canal will be dispensed with as the new bridge will have sufficient height to allow clearance for the passage of canal traffic.

definitions.definition: The right to pass from one place to another.
A fee paid for passing or for being conveyed between places.
(bacteriology, virology) Serial passage.
(dice games, historical) A gambling game for two players using three dice, in which the object is to throw a double over ten. [from 15th c.]
(medicine) To pass something, such as a pathogen or stem cell, through a host or medium.
(rare) To make a passage, especially by sea; to cross.
(falconry, attributive) Of a bird: Less than a year old but living on its own, having left the nest.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French passager, from Italian passeggiare.

definitions.definition: (dressage) A movement in classical dressage, in which the horse performs a very collected, energetic, and elevated trot that has a longer period of suspension between each foot fall than a working trot.
(intransitive, dressage) To execute a passage movement.

quote.text: After a spring or two, the horse passaged and reared, and lighting on a flat slab of rock which cropped up in the middle of the road, slipped sideways and fell with a loud crash  […]
